title: The Pipeline Is Dead - Iris ten Teije, Sky Valley Ambient Computing

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on AI code generation as the main product and research object, dissolving the development-distribution boundary through per-user adaptive software. Differ is developer infrastructure for adaptive software, and the paradigm shift applies across all software verticals. The talk spans development, distribution, runtime adaptation, testing, and observability of per-user software divergences. Advanced architectural tradeoffs in lineage, isolation, testing, and coordination remain unsolved. Conference talk with architectural discussion and frontier challenges. All evidence anchors are directly stated in the transcript.

summary: Iris ten Teije, co-founder of Differ (with co-founder Noam, first engineer at JFrog), argues that the entire software distribution stack—CI pipelines, packagers, registries, container images, app store reviews—exists to solve one problem: safely and reproducibly moving a frozen artifact from the build machine to the run machine. This stack encodes a single assumption: one version of your software for everyone. This was never a deliberate decision but the only viable shape because producing a correct change was expensive and risky, requiring skilled humans hours or days. Freezing one artifact gave reproducibility, previewability, and rollback, but the price was software that couldn't be for anyone in particular. The cost of producing correct, scoped changes is now collapsing toward zero, and production no longer must happen in one place upfront—it can occur on the server, client, or in the user's live session. As making a change becomes as cheap as running one and happens in the same place, the reason to separate development from distribution dissolves. Demand for personalized software has always existed: forward-deployed engineers, hand-tuned dotfiles, and Excel's millions of user-built programs. Feature flags and A/B testing were early divergence attempts but forced into pre-declared buckets. Differ's architecture deploys one canonical stem with bounded, isolated, individually reversible per-user divergences; developers set boundaries on what can and cannot be adapted (e.g., auth and payments off-limits). Hard challenges include source of truth, lineage as a graph query, correctness, testing across all divergences, desirability (measuring whether a change was an actual improvement against company-specific goals), autonomy versus control (winning trust so humans choose to step back rather than building more control), and coordination across millions of versions. The recurring answer to coordination is: don't merge code, merge intent and outcome—everyone converges on the same goal through their own path. Iris emphasizes that code generation is the easy 80%; the hard part is the substrate—stem plus divergences, provenance, validation, observability, and coordination. She closes with analogies to fintech (branchless banks once seemed reckless) and CI (Noam fought engineers about needing builds), framing adaptive software as the same type of inevitable shift. The pipeline didn't fail; the constraint it was built for went away.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Pipeline Assumption: One Version for Everyone
sections.summary: Iris opens by asking how many in the audience have spent careers moving software between machines. The entire distribution stack—CI, packagers, registries, containers, app stores—solves one problem: getting a frozen artifact from build to run machine, once. The unchallenged assumption is one version of your software for everyone.

sections.title: Why the Pipeline Existed: Expensive Production
sections.summary: The one-way pipeline is a direct consequence of software production being expensive and risky. Producing a correct change took skilled humans hours or days, so it was rare, central, verified, and frozen. The frozen artifact gave reproducibility, previewability, and rollback, but the price was software that couldn't be for anyone in particular. A version per user was never an option because it meant forking and hand-maintaining codebases.

sections.title: Cost Collapse and the Dissolving Boundary
sections.summary: The cost of producing correct, scoped changes is collapsing toward zero. Production no longer must happen in one place upfront—parts can run on the server, client, or in the user's live session. As making a change becomes as cheap as running one and happens in the same place, the reason to separate development from distribution dissolves.

sections.title: Demand Side: Personalized Software Is Not New
sections.summary: People have always wanted software that fits them. Evidence: enterprise professional services and forward-deployed engineers for big clients, hand-tuned dotfiles and editor configs rebuilt on every machine, and Excel as millions of user-built programs. Feature flags, segmentation, and A/B testing were early divergence attempts but forced into pre-declared buckets. Now coding agents enable true adaptation at the software layer.

sections.title: Differ's Architecture: Stem Plus Bounded Divergences
sections.summary: When the agent is the runtime, development and distribution merge. Differ's shape: one canonical stem, each user runs their own divergence—same origin, individually adapted live. A CTO's objection about running millions of AI-generated codebases is addressed: the brittleness people fear is unmanaged divergence inside a single tangled artifact. Differ ships one stem plus bounded, isolated, reversible divergences. Blast radius is one context; any divergence rolls back with no deploy.

sections.title: Developer Controls and CRM Example
sections.summary: Developers set boundaries on what can and cannot be adapted—auth and payments stay off-limits, specific form fields can be marked non-droppable. A CRM example: an investor logs founder intros, so the system creates an intro-path field; hides fields she never fills; reprioritizes deal listings based on observed patterns. Users can also proactively request changes within developer-set boundaries, enabling horizontal SaaS to address more personas without increased R&D spend.

sections.title: Hard Challenges: Source of Truth and Lineage
sections.summary: With no single artifact, source of truth becomes the stem plus all divergences. Lineage becomes a graph query rather than a version number—what is this user running and why? Bug reports describe a program that exists for one specific user. Every divergence must be immutable, inspectable, attributable, and traceable back to the signal that produced the adaptation. Correctness is raised as a further challenge.

sections.title: Testing, Desirability, Autonomy, and Coordination
sections.summary: Testing must reason about the stem and every possible divergence. Desirability asks whether a change was actually an improvement against company-specific goals (retention, churn, support tickets). Autonomy versus control: the vision is a system that acts without asking permission every time; the challenge is winning enough trust that humans choose to step back. Coordination across millions of versions: the recurring answer is don't merge code, merge intent and outcome—everyone converges on the same goal through their own path.

sections.title: Generation Is the Easy 80%; The Substrate Is the Business
sections.summary: Iris clarifies that code generation has become easy—calling a model to write code is something everyone can do. The hard part is observability, validation, coordination, provenance, and the stem-plus-divergences substrate. That is the entire business and what Differ works on every day.

sections.title: Closing: The Shift Is Inevitable
sections.summary: Iris closes with analogies: branchless banks once seemed reckless, Noam fought engineers about needing CI. Adaptive software is the same type of shift—it doesn't feel obvious until it does. The pipeline didn't fail because it stopped working; the constraint it was built for went away. Twenty years were spent shipping one version for everyone; the next twenty are about shipping the right version to anyone with isolation and provenance that makes it safe instead of terrifying.

demonstrations: CRM adapted for an investor: system observes intro-logging behavior and creates an intro-path field; hides unused fields; reprioritizes deal listings based on observed patterns.
Form adaptation for conversion rate with developer constraints that specific fields can never be dropped.
Developer boundary controls: auth and payments marked off-limits for any adaptation.
limitations: Testing at scale requires reasoning about the stem and every possible divergence of it—an unsolved challenge.
Desirability: knowing whether a change was actually an improvement (uplift) against company-specific goals is hard to measure and track.
Autonomy versus control: building a system good, legible, and reliable enough that humans choose to step back is an ongoing hard problem.
Coordination across millions of versions: how changes propagate to a million different versions—the proposed answer is merge intent not code, but implementation is still being worked on.
Correctness verification for per-user divergences remains a hard challenge.
quantitativeClaims: Producing a correct change used to take skilled humans hours or days.
Cost of producing a correct, scoped change is collapsing toward zero.
A million per-user versions can be more contained than a single tangled codebase.
Code generation is the easy 80%; the substrate and coordination are the hard 20% that constitute the business.

evidence.excerpt: That entire stack exists to solve exactly one problem. Get a frozen artifact, that code, from machine where it was built to the machine where it runs, safely, reproducibly, once.
evidence.supports: The distribution stack exists to move one frozen artifact from build to run machine.

evidence.excerpt: Giving to users different software meant forking the code base and hand maintaining both. A version per user at any real scale wasn't really a viable option.
evidence.supports: A version per user was never an option because it required forking and hand-maintaining codebases.

evidence.excerpt: the production of the software no longer has to happen in one place up front before anyone runs it. Part of it can be run on the server, part of it on the client, part in the user's live session.
evidence.supports: Software production can now happen at runtime across server, client, and user session.

evidence.excerpt: instead of one code base gated by flags and shipped to everyone, you deploy one canonical stem and every user runs her own divergence of it. Same origin, but individually adapted live.
evidence.supports: Differ's architecture deploys one canonical stem with per-user divergences.

evidence.excerpt: The divergences are bounded, isolated, and individually reversible. A bad variant can silently corrupt the stem or reach another user. Which means that the blast radius of a changes in the system is one context.
evidence.supports: Divergences are bounded, isolated, reversible, with blast radius of one context.

evidence.excerpt: What is this user running and why? That now becomes more of a graph query versus a version number. A bug report describes a program that exists for that specific user.
evidence.supports: Lineage becomes a graph query; debugging targets a per-user program.

evidence.excerpt: testing at a much larger scale of users means that you need to reason about the stem and also every possible divergence of it.
evidence.supports: Testing requires reasoning about the stem and every possible divergence.

evidence.excerpt: anyone can make a code change now, but the hard part is knowing whether you actually found an improvement, an uplift.
evidence.supports: Desirability—knowing whether a change was actually an improvement—is a hard challenge.

evidence.excerpt: don't merge code, merge intent, merge outcome. Which means not everyone has to run the same commit or this exact same piece of code, but everyone converges on the same goal through their own path.
evidence.supports: Coordination answer: merge intent and outcome rather than code.

evidence.excerpt: Generation has become easy, and I would say that's actually the easy 80%. Calling a model to write some code is something that everyone can do. The other part, observability, validation, coordination, that is the entire business.
evidence.supports: Code generation is the easy 80%; the substrate and coordination are the business.

evidence.excerpt: We spent 20 years getting good at shipping one version for everyone. The next 20 years are about shipping the right version to anyone with the isolation and provenance that makes it safe instead of terrifying.
evidence.supports: The next era of software distribution is per-user versions with isolation and provenance.
